reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations
chapter_title: Overview of Pile Foundation Design and Construction

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Opens with Peck's remark that driving piles is 'a crude and brutal process': pile-soil and pile-rock interaction is complex, broad generalizations about pile behavior are unrealistic, and practical semi-empirical methods are needed. The engineer must understand the subsurface conditions, the limit states, the factored loads and combinations, the performance requirements, costs and local practice.
sections.body: (p. 7) Quoting Professor R. B. Peck, driving piles for a foundation is 'a crude and brutal process.' Pile insertion alters the soil and sets up intense local strains; soil non-homogeneity, group effects and pile shape add difficulty, and for piles driven to or into rock the rock mass structure (joints, bedding planes, weathering) complicates rock-pile interaction. Broad generalizations about pile behavior are unrealistic, so practical semi-empirical design methods are used, with attention on significant factors rather than minor details. To reach the optimum driven pile solution the foundation engineer must understand the subsurface conditions (soil and rock parameters and behavior), the applicable limit states, the factored loads and load combinations, the project performance requirements, foundation costs, and current design and construction practice where the foundation is located.
key_points: Peck: driving piles for a foundation is 'a crude and brutal process'
Pile insertion alters the soil; non-homogeneity, group effects and pile shape complicate soil-pile interaction
For piles to hard rock or into soft rock, joints, bedding planes and weathering complicate rock-pile interaction
Broad generalizations about pile behavior are unrealistic; practical semi-empirical methods are necessary
The engineer needs the subsurface conditions, limit states, factored loads, performance requirements, costs and local practice
sections.applicability: General introduction to the LRFD-based driven pile design and construction process for all highway structure foundations.

sections.title: Limit States
sections.summary: AASHTO (2014) identifies four limit states (strength, service, extreme event, fatigue) with up to thirteen load combination cases (Table 2-1). Strength I, Strength IV, Extreme Event I (earthquake), Extreme Event II (ice, vessel, blast, vehicle collision) and Service I commonly govern driven pile design; all applicable limit states have equal importance. Service II-IV and Fatigue I-II relate to superstructure elements.
sections.body: (pp. 7-8) The AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (AASHTO 2014) identify four limit states: strength, service, extreme event and fatigue. With their load combination cases, up to thirteen limit states may need evaluation in a bridge design: five strength, two extreme event, four service and two fatigue cases (Table 2-1). Limit states that commonly govern driven pile foundation design are Strength I, Strength IV, Extreme Event I (earthquake), Extreme Event II (ice, vessel, blast and vehicle collision) and Service I. All applicable limit states have equal importance. Service II, III and IV and Fatigue I and II relate to superstructure elements and are not generally applicable to foundation design.
key_points: Four AASHTO limit states: strength, service, extreme event and fatigue
Up to thirteen cases: five strength, two extreme event, four service and two fatigue (Table 2-1)
Strength I, Strength IV, Extreme Event I and II, and Service I commonly govern driven pile foundations
Strength IV: very high dead to live load force effect ratios (typical for spans greater than 250 ft)
All applicable limit states have equal importance in the design
Service II, III, IV and Fatigue I, II are generally not applicable to foundation design

sections.applicability: Identifying which AASHTO limit states apply to driven pile foundation design. Used at the beginning of any pile design to establish required checks.

sections.title: Loads, Load Combinations, and Load Factors
sections.summary: Total factored load Q = sum(eta_i gamma_i Q_i) (Eq. 2-1); each limit state has its load combination (Table 2-2) and the permanent load factor gamma_p has maximum and minimum values (Table 2-3), the more critical one selected (DC 1.25/0.90, DD by Tomlinson alpha 1.40/0.25, DD by lambda 1.05/0.30). Structural analysis gives the column-cap reactions as axial, lateral and moment force effects, iterated with the geotechnical analysis (Figure 2-1); Figure 2-2 is a worked example.
sections.body: (pp. 9-13) The total factored load Q for a limit state follows from the force effects, load modifiers and load factors (Eq. 2-1). A specific load combination applies for each limit state case (Table 2-2); the two-letter codes in its second column are permanent loads and the rest transient loads. For Strength I, Q = gamma_p (DC + DD + DW + EH + EV + ES + EL + PS + CR + SH) + 1.75 (LL + IM + CE + BR + PL + LS) + WA + FR + 1.20 TU + gamma_TG TG + gamma_SE SE. The permanent load factor gamma_p has maximum and minimum values (Table 2-3), and the one producing the more critical combination is selected. Following Brown et al. (2010), the structural engineer finds the foundation force effects for each limit state from a preliminary structural model under the Table 2-2 combinations with factored loads; the column-cap reactions are resolved into vertical, horizontal and moment components taken as the factored axial, lateral and moment force effects at the top of the cap (Figure 2-1). Multiple iterations bring the structural and geotechnical deformations and forces into agreement at the column-cap interface, and the load factors are varied over their ranges to find the maximum force effects. Figure 2-2 gives the loads for a 45 ft wide, three span, 350 ft long structure with a 100 ft main span subject to scour and seismic events: at Abutment 1, 2548 kips (Strength I) and 1982 kips (Service II) axial and 1980 kips transverse shear (Extreme Event I); at Pier 2, 5542 kips (Strength I) and 4307 kips (Service II) axial, 1267 kips longitudinal shear and 40,800 ft-kips moment (Extreme Event I). Each combination is checked independently against the factored resistance and tolerable deformations.

Table 2-2 gives the load combination and load factors for each limit state

Table 2-3: DC 1.25/0.90 (Strength IV only 1.50/0.90); DD Tomlinson alpha 1.40/0.25; DD lambda 1.05/0.30; DW 1.50/0.90
Table 2-3: EH active 1.50/0.90, at-rest 1.35/0.90; EV retaining walls and abutments 1.35/1.00; ES 1.50/0.75
Use the maximum or minimum gamma_p, whichever gives the more critical combination
Column-cap reactions become the factored axial, lateral and moment force effects at the top of the cap (Figure 2-1)
Structural and geotechnical analyses are iterated until deformations and forces agree at the interface
Figure 2-2 example: Pier 2 at 5542 kips axial (Strength I) and 40,800 ft-kips moment (Extreme Event I)

sections.applicability: Determining factored foundation loads for all limit states. Used at the start of pile design to establish demand. Structural engineer provides these loads to the foundation specialist.

sections.title: Nominal and Factored Resistance
sections.summary: LRFD check: sum(eta_i*gamma_i*Q_i) <= phi*R_n = R_r (Eq 2-2). Factored resistance is the lesser of factored structural and geotechnical resistance. Redundancy: >=5 piles per cap is redundant; <=4 is non-redundant and requires 20% resistance factor reduction per AASHTO C10.5.5.2.3.
sections.body: (p. 14) The nominal resistance R_n is calculated and multiplied by the resistance factor phi to determine the factored resistance R_r. The basic LRFD methodology equation (Eq. 2-2) requires that the factored resistance be greater than or equal to the sum of all factored force effects. Nominal geotechnical resistances and resistance factors are discussed in Chapter 7. Paikowsky (2004) in NCHRP Report 507 defined redundancy based on the number of piles per cap: 5 or more piles is redundant, 4 or fewer is non-redundant. For non-redundant designs, AASHTO Article C10.5.5.2.3 recommends reducing the resistance factor by 20%. The load modifiers for redundancy (AASHTO Article 1.3.4) were developed for superstructures.
key_points: Basic LRFD equation: sum(eta_i * gamma_i * Q_i) <= phi * R_n = R_r
phi is the resistance factor, a statistically based multiplier applied to nominal resistance
Factored resistance must be >= sum of all factored force effects for all limit states
Redundant piles: 5 or more per pile cap; non-redundant: 4 or fewer per pile cap
Non-redundant designs: reduce resistance factor by 20% per AASHTO C10.5.5.2.3
Factored resistance is the lesser of factored structural or factored geotechnical resistance
Geotechnical resistance factors vary by resistance determination method (Chapter 7)
Structural resistance factors are presented in Chapter 8
equations: Eq. 2-2: sum(eta_i gamma_i Q_i) <= phi R_n = R_r; eta_i = load modifier; gamma_i = load factor; Q_i = force effect; phi = resistance factor; R_n = nominal resistance; R_r = factored resistance (p. 14)
sections.applicability: Core LRFD resistance check for all driven pile designs. Applied when comparing factored loads to factored resistances at strength, service, and extreme event limit states.

sections.title: Strength Limit States
sections.summary: Strength limit state checks for driven piles: axial compression and uplift resistance for single piles and groups, lateral resistance, bearing stratum punching, structural resistance under combined axial and flexural loading, drivability including driving stresses, and loss of support due to design flood scour (100-year event).
sections.body: (p. 15) The strength limit states ensure local and global strength and stability against statistically significant load combinations during the structure design life. Strength limit state design includes evaluation of nominal geotechnical and structural resistances as well as loss of lateral and vertical support due to scour in the design flood event (100 year). Geotechnical and structural strength limit state considerations are described in detail in Chapters 7 and 8.
key_points: Axial compression resistance of single piles and pile groups
Uplift resistance of single piles and pile groups
Lateral resistance of single piles and pile groups
Bearing stratum punching failure
Structural resistance in axial compression, combined axial and flexural loading, and shear
Drivability including driving stresses
Loss of lateral and vertical support due to design flood scour (100 year event)
sections.applicability: Checking geotechnical and structural strength for driven pile foundations under Strength I through V load combinations. Detailed methods in Chapters 7 (geotechnical) and 8 (structural).

sections.title: Service Limit States
sections.summary: Service limit state checks: vertical settlement of single piles and groups, horizontal movements under lateral loads, rotation of pile groups, overall stability, and deformations due to 100-year scour. All applicable Service I load combinations must be evaluated per AASHTO Articles 10.5.2.1–10.5.2.4.
sections.body: (p. 15) The service limit states provide limits on stress, deformation, and cracking under regular service conditions. Service limit state considerations in driven pile foundation designs include vertical deformation (settlement), horizontal movements, rotation, overall stability, and deformations due to scour at the design flood (100 year event). All applicable service limit state load combinations must be evaluated per AASHTO (2014) Articles 10.5.2.1 through 10.5.2.4.
key_points: Vertical deformation (settlement) of single piles and pile groups
Horizontal movements under lateral loads
Rotation of pile groups and foundations
Overall stability of the foundation system
Deformations due to scour at the 100-year design flood
All applicable service limit state load combinations must be evaluated
sections.applicability: Checking deformations and serviceability of driven pile foundations under Service I load combination. Settlement analysis (Chapter 7) and lateral deformation analysis (Chapter 7, Section 7.3.4) apply.

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit States
sections.summary: Extreme Event I (seismic) and Extreme Event II (500-year flood scour, vessel collision, vehicle collision, blast) checks. Liquefaction assessment required for multi-span bridges in Seismic Zones 2, 3, or 4. Seismic design per GEC-3 and AASHTO Section 10, Appendix A10.
sections.body: (p. 16) Extreme event limit states ensure structural survival of a bridge under unique major occurrences such as earthquakes, floods, vehicle and vessel collisions, or blasts with return periods significantly greater than the bridge design life. A liquefaction assessment is required as part of the design for multi-span bridges if the site is classified as Seismic Zone 2, 3, or 4. Extreme event limit states are discussed further in Section 7.4 of this manual.
key_points: Check flood (500 year event) for scour
Vessel collision
Vehicle collision
Blast loading
Seismic loading (earthquake)
Liquefaction assessment required for multi-span bridges in Seismic Zone 2, 3, or 4
Other site-specific situations determined by the design engineer
sections.applicability: Evaluating driven pile foundations under Extreme Event I (earthquake) and Extreme Event II (ice, vessel, blast, vehicle collision) load combinations. Seismic design per GEC-3 and AASHTO Section 10, Appendix A10.

sections.title: Construction of Pile Foundations
sections.summary: Successful construction requires relating load requirements to field resistance determination methods. Wave equation analysis, dynamic monitoring, and static load tests verify nominal resistance. Post-construction review of driving results versus predictions is essential for quality assurance and future design improvement.
sections.body: (pp. 16-17) Construction of a successful driven pile foundation depends on relating load requirements to resistance requirements of the field installation and resistance determination method. A pile foundation must meet limit state requirements for compressive, lateral, and uplift resistance. Wave equation analysis, dynamic monitoring of pile driving, and/or static load testing can all be used to verify nominal resistance and avoid pile damage or cost overruns. Post-construction review of driving results versus predictions regarding resistances, pile lengths, and field problems is essential.
key_points: Design and construction must be explicitly incorporated into plans and specifications
Piles must meet compressive, lateral, and uplift resistance requirements
Wave equation analysis, dynamic monitoring, and static load tests verify field resistance
Agencies have calibrated new dynamic formulas to replace unreliable ones (e.g., Engineering News formula)
Knowledgeable construction supervision and inspection are keys to proper pile installation
Post-construction review of driving results versus predictions is essential
LRFD implementation allows post-construction data to improve resistance factors for future projects
sections.applicability: Construction phase of driven pile projects. Addresses field verification of nominal resistance and quality assurance. Detailed in Chapters 12 (wave equation), 14 (specifications), and 18 (inspection).

sections.title: Foundation Specialist Involvement
sections.summary: A foundation specialist with both structural and geotechnical expertise is essential from planning through post-construction. The specialist is best positioned to select pile type, estimate pile length, and choose the most cost-effective resistance determination method. Continuity of specialist involvement applies to all contracting methods.
sections.body: (pp. 17-18) The input of an experienced foundation specialist is essential to produce a successful driven pile foundation. A foundation specialist has both structural and geotechnical background in design and construction. The specialist is the most knowledgeable person for selecting pile type, estimating pile length, and choosing the most appropriate and cost-effective resistance determination method. The foundation specialist should be involved from the planning stage through the design and construction process.
key_points: Foundation specialist has both structural and geotechnical expertise
Most knowledgeable person for pile type selection, length estimation, and resistance method choice
Should be involved from planning stage through construction
Significant involvement in preliminary explorations, preliminary design, and final design phases
Technical support role during construction and post-construction review
Provides continuity of design personnel through construction stage
Importance of continuity applies to all types of contracting methods
sections.applicability: All project phases from planning through post-construction. Defines the interdisciplinary role of the foundation specialist in driven pile projects.

sections.title: The Driven Pile Design and Construction Process
sections.summary: 32-block design-construction flow chart (Fig 2-3) covering planning (Blocks 1–8), preliminary design (9–19), design refinement (20–27), and construction (28–32). Lead roles identified by block border: structural engineer (solid), geotechnical engineer (dashed), construction engineer (dash-dot). Dynamic resistance methods are generally more accurate than static analysis.
sections.body:
(pp. 18-39) The driven pile design and construction process is outlined in the 32-block flow chart of Figure 2-3. Static analysis from the subsurface exploration has the primary function of estimating the pile length for bidding; the driving criterion is usually a blow count set early in installation, sometimes with a minimum penetration depth for uplift, lateral load or serviceability. The process includes aspects unique to all structural design because pile driving characteristics can improve the accuracy of geotechnical resistance estimates. Dynamic methods for determining nominal resistance from penetration data or dynamic measurements are generally more accurate than static analysis methods based on subsurface exploration. Pile drivability must be considered during the design phase to avoid costly construction problems. The flow chart distinguishes lead roles by block border style: structural engineer (solid), geotechnical engineer (dashed), and construction engineer (dash-dot). The process covers planning (Blocks 1-8), preliminary design (Blocks 9-19), design refinement (Blocks 20-27), and construction (Blocks 28-32).

Preliminary design (Blocks 9-19): The preliminary design phase begins with calculating nominal and factored structural resistances (Block 9), then geotechnical resistances in compression and tension versus depth with preliminary drivability analysis (Block 10). Individual pile loads are resolved at all limit states (Block 11). Penetration depths are established for axial compression (Block 12), tension (Block 13), lateral loads (Block 14), and tolerable deformations based on group settlement (Block 15). Drivability is checked for all candidate pile types (Block 16) within a reasonable blow count of 30 to 120 blows/ft; 120 blows/ft (10 blows/inch) is refusal for many hammer manufacturers, so depending on the expected driving conditions an upper limit of 96 blows/ft (8 blows/inch) may be more reasonable. The neutral plane location and drag force are determined (Block 17), settlement is verified (Block 18), and economics are evaluated (Block 19).

Design refinement (Blocks 20-27): After preliminary design is complete at all substructure locations (Block 20), structural modeling is refined with updated foundation top loads and lateral earth pressure loads on abutments (Block 21). If loads change significantly, foundation design is re-evaluated (Block 22). For dynamic elastic analyses (seismic), foundation stiffnesses are re-evaluated using unfactored loads (Block 23) and loads are checked for convergence within 5% (Block 24). The final design must meet all limit state requirements (Block 25). Pile caps are designed per AASHTO concrete specifications (Block 26). Plans and specifications are finalized with pile quantities, minimum penetration requirements, required nominal resistances, resistance determination method, and resistance factor phi_dyn (Block 27).

Construction (Blocks 28-32): Construction begins with evaluation of the contractor's proposed equipment (Block 28). Wave equation analysis estimates the blow count to meet required nominal driving resistance and checks if the pile can be driven to the required depth without exceeding material stress limits. Preliminary driving criteria are set and test piles are driven (Block 29). Driving requirements may be defined by blow count, minimum penetration depth, dynamic monitoring results, or a combination. Each field resistance determination method has its own resistance factor phi_dyn. If test results indicate inadequate resistance, driving criteria or design may be adjusted (Block 30). Production piles are driven with construction monitoring (Block 31), and post-construction evaluation is performed for design refinement on future projects (Block 32). (The section runs from printed p. 18 to p. 39 with no numbered subsections; the blocks are its steps.)
key_points: Figure 2-3: a 32-block flow chart; lead roles shown by border style (structural, geotechnical, construction engineer)
Planning (Blocks 1-8): performance requirements, geometry, site conditions, exploration, candidate foundation systems, 2-5 candidate pile types
Preliminary design (Blocks 9-19): structural and geotechnical resistance vs depth, penetration for compression, tension, lateral load and deformation
Block 16: eliminate candidates not drivable within 30-120 blows/ft; 120 blows/ft is refusal, 96 blows/ft (8 blows/in) may be a better upper limit
Block 17: neutral plane and drag force; permanent load plus drag force below the factored structural resistance
Block 19: compare candidates on cost per unit load supported, including caps and cofferdams
Design refinement (Blocks 20-27): refine the structural model, re-check loads (convergence within 5 % for seismic), design caps, finalize plans
Block 27: plans show the factored load, nominal resistance, resistance determination method, phi_dyn and minimum penetration
Construction (Blocks 28-32): wave equation check of the contractor's equipment, test piles, driving criteria, production driving, post-construction review
Changing the resistance determination method changes both the resistance factor and the required nominal resistance
Pile drivability must be considered during design
Preliminary field testing before final design can save substantially on large projects
figures: Figure 2-3: Driven pile design and construction process (pp. 19-24, continued over six pages)
sections.applicability: Complete design-construction process for driven pile foundations. Figure 2-3 flow chart applies to all design-bid-build projects; design-build contracts vary in early steps but the key activities remain the same.

sections.title: Communication
sections.summary: Interdisciplinary communication between structural, geotechnical, hydraulic, geologic, and construction engineers is essential throughout driven pile design and construction. Tables 2-4 and 2-5 identify which disciplines must communicate at each stage. Construction-stage items (QC/QA, wave equation, load testing, installation problems) require all three disciplines.
sections.body: (pp. 39-41) Good communication between all organizations and disciplines involved in the design and construction of a pile foundation is essential for successful project completion. In the design stage, communication and interaction is needed between the structural, geotechnical, geologic, hydraulic, and construction disciplines, as well as with consultants, drill crews, and laboratory personnel. In the construction stage, structural, geotechnical, and construction disciplines must communicate for timely resolution of construction issues. Tables 2-4 and 2-5 detail the key communication items in both design and construction stages.
key_points: Communication between structural, geotechnical, hydraulic, geologic, and construction disciplines is essential

Design stage: loads and performance criteria, scour potential, extreme events, past construction problems, exploration programs, pile type/length/resistance, construction QA methods, approach fill effects, plans/specs
Construction stage: construction control and QA, wave equation analysis of contractor's driving system, static/dynamic load testing, and resolution of pile installation problems
Table 2-4 shows which disciplines are involved in each design stage communication item
Table 2-5 shows which disciplines are involved in each construction stage communication item
All four construction stage items require involvement of structural, geotechnical, and construction disciplines
